features.title: Review threads and anchors
features.summary: Review threads as canonical Workspace resources: what a thread is anchored to and its Variant scope, invalid anchors and explicit re-anchoring, retention, the Workbench thread timeline, and how threads are summarized, listed and filtered.

rules.statement: A Review thread's identity is independent of the View and Widget it concerns, its text and its position in any list, so re-anchoring or editing a thread never changes its identity.
A Widget anchor names its target only by stable View and Widget identity, never by DOM selector, rendered geometry, child index or tree path, so moving the Widget within its View keeps the anchor.
A comment about a whole View is anchored to that View's RootShell Widget.
Feedback about the product as a whole is anchored to the Workspace itself and names no View or Widget.
Creating a thread always states its anchor; an omitted anchor never defaults to the Workspace.
A Widget thread's Variant scope limits it to the named Variants of its View, and an empty scope means every current and future Variant.
A named Variant in a thread's scope that no longer exists makes that part of the anchor invalid, and the thread is kept.
When a thread's anchored View or Widget no longer exists, the thread is kept unchanged with an invalid anchor; deleting the target never resolves, moves or deletes it.
The Workbench shows a thread whose anchor is invalid with a missing-target notice that offers explicit repair.
UIUX never binds a thread to another target by DOM selector, tree position, geometry or similarity, and non-authoritative display hints never decide a thread's target.
A Workspace anchor always resolves, so a Workspace thread never has an invalid anchor.
Only an explicit re-anchor changes a thread's anchor or Variant scope.
A re-anchor may move a thread from a Widget to the Workspace, from the Workspace to a Widget, or within either, including to the anchor it already has.
Every re-anchor appends an immutable history event with the previous and new anchor and Variant scope, so earlier anchors stay in the thread's history.
No Workbench or MCP action deletes a Review thread except the author's retraction of an unengaged thread, and resolved threads stay stored as design history.
A reply appends a new message to the end of the thread's messages, on a thread of any status.
A Review thread's list item summarizes its anchor, Variant scope, pin hint, status, current resolution and latest activity, and briefly its latest message and current submission.
A thread's latest activity is the newest authored time among its messages, message edits, submissions and history events.
Listing and searching Review threads accept structured filters for status, View, anchor validity, Variant scope, change or Evidence domain, current resolution and anchor scope.

The Workbench shows a thread as one chronological timeline of its messages, re-anchor events, submissions and lifecycle events, each keeping its own type and content, derived from the thread rather than stored.
In the Workbench a reviewer can start a Workspace thread from the Reviews inbox and from the command palette.

features.title: Review lifecycle and resolution
features.summary: The lifecycle of a Review thread: ready-for-review submissions and their Evidence gate, resolution and its kinds, reopening, and how the Workbench offers resolution.

rules.statement: Every lifecycle transition appends an immutable event to the thread's history, and the thread's current status always matches the latest one.
Marking a thread ready for review records a new immutable submission; it means work was submitted, not that it was accepted.
Every entry into ready for review, including one after a reopen, appends a new submission and never replaces an earlier one.
Once a submission exists, its change domains, resources and Evidence references never change.
A Widget thread can enter ready for review only while its anchored View is valid as a whole and every named Variant is executable.
A Widget thread's submission names its anchored View at that View's current revision.
A Workspace thread's submission names the current Workspace manifest revision as its subject.
Every View a Workspace thread's submission names must exist, be valid and be named at its current revision.
Every Evidence reference of a submission must name an Evidence record that exists in the Workspace.
Formal-capture Evidence cited by a submission must be complete for the current revision of the View it captured, and that View must belong to the submission's target set.
An Evidence reference whose declared kind differs from the referenced record's kind is invalid and diagnosed, never coerced or rewritten.

A visual or interaction change cites Playwright captures of the clean Preview Host in the affected render and Variant contexts; a purely textual Spec change needs no capture but still needs passing validation.
An interaction change cites replayable interaction Evidence of structured steps, targets and assertions replayed with Playwright; screenshots alone never verify interaction.
Resolving a ready-for-review thread without naming a resolution resolves it as verified, accepting its latest submission.
Resolving an open thread requires an explicit resolution; the API never chooses one for the caller.
Closing a ready-for-review thread with any resolution other than verified leaves its pending submission in the thread, not accepted.
UIUX never checks a resolution against other resources: whether a thread is obsolete or a duplicate is the resolving human's judgment.
Reopening a thread, whatever its resolution, keeps its earlier lifecycle events and submissions unchanged in its history.
After a reopen, a verified resolution needs a new submission: an earlier verified resolution is never carried forward.
In the Workbench, the one-click Resolve resolves an open thread as answered and accepts a ready-for-review thread's submission as verified, naming that submission.
The Workbench's Resolve menu groups answered and verified under Resolve, and obsolete, duplicate and won't-fix under Dismiss; the grouping is presentation only.
For a thread whose anchor is invalid, the Workbench offers resolving it as obsolete but never chooses that resolution without the user.
The timeline shows each resolution with its kind, and marks a submission declined by a non-verified close as not accepted.

features.title: Review message editing
features.summary: Editing Review messages: who may edit and until when, how earlier versions are kept, and how edits appear in the Workbench.

rules.statement: Only a message's author, human or Agent, may replace its text; no other member, an Owner included, may edit it.
Authorship is proven by the edit's stamped actor matching the message's actor, so a message written before stamping or by a removed member can never be edited.
A message is frozen permanently once a ready-for-review submission or a resolution exists at or after its authored time; reopening the thread never unfreezes it.
Messages written after the latest submission or resolution stay editable, even on a resolved thread.
Apart from the freeze, editing a message has no time limit.
Each edit keeps the replaced text append-only on the message, with the edit's server-stamped actor and time.
An edited message keeps its authored time and timeline position; an edit adds no history event and no separate timeline item.
No Review action deletes a single message.
An edited thread shows as unread to members who saw it before the edit.
Search matches a message's current text only, never its earlier versions.
The Workbench marks an edited message as edited, with the edit time, and lets every reader of the thread open its earlier versions, newest first, read-only.
On the viewer's own frozen message, the Workbench shows Edit as unavailable with the reason.
Editing a message never changes a Decision promoted from its thread, and promotion does not freeze messages.

features.title: Review thread retraction
features.summary: Hard deletion of a brand-new Review thread before anyone engages with it: who may retract, when a thread is eligible, what remains afterwards, and the Workbench affordance.

rules.statement: Only the author of a thread's single message may retract the thread, whether a human or an Agent.
A thread whose message was written before actors were stamped cannot be retracted, because no stamp can prove its authorship.
A thread can be retracted only while it is open, holds at most one message, has no history events or submissions, and no Decision was promoted from it.
A thread with no messages, which has no author, may be retracted by any Reviewer under the same conditions.
The author's own edits and any move of the pin are not engagement and never block retraction.
Retraction removes the thread file atomically and leaves no trace in canonical state: no tombstone, history entry or record of who retracted it.

Eligibility is checked on exactly the thread revision being deleted, inside the delete's exclusive lock, so a racing reply or promotion either lands first and makes retraction refuse, or finds the thread gone.
After retraction, reads and writes of the thread report it as not found.
Copies of a retracted thread inside already-exported Handoff bundles remain; retraction never scans or rewrites artifacts.
The Workbench offers to delete a comment only to its author while the loaded thread is eligible, and offers to delete an empty thread to any Reviewer.
The Workbench confirms a deletion in an inline row with focus on Cancel, never in a browser dialog.
A link to a retracted thread opens the inbox's missing-thread state, or on the canvas the View with a notice that the comment no longer exists.

features.title: Comment pins
features.summary: Comment pins on the Workbench canvas: the optional persisted pin hint and how it is set, moved, cleared and kept out of other records, where pins are drawn, and when they are hidden.

rules.statement: A thread's pin hint is display data only: anchor resolution, validity, comparison, filtering and re-anchoring never read it.
A pin hint is never validated against the View, the Widget's existence or size, a Variant or a render context.
Creating a thread may set its pin hint; a thread without one draws its pin at the default placement.
A re-anchor that supplies a hint sets it and one that clears the hint clears it; otherwise the hint is cleared when the Widget changes and kept when only the Variant scope changes.
Re-anchoring a thread to the Workspace always clears its pin hint.
Moving or clearing a thread's pin within its Widget is a separate action that never changes the anchor, records no actor and appends no history event.
The Workbench writes a moved pin once, when the drag ends, never streaming intermediate positions.
Pin hints never enter lifecycle or re-anchor history, submissions, Evidence records, formal captures or Decision provenance.
Re-anchoring back to an earlier Widget never restores the hint the thread had there.
A hinted pin is drawn at the hint's point within the anchored Widget's current rendered rectangle, so it follows the Widget when it resizes or reflows, in every viewport.
Pin hints are physical coordinates, so a pin keeps its side in a right-to-left Locale.

A pin is hidden, never clamped or moved elsewhere, when its point is clipped or occluded, its Widget is not rendered, the geometry is stale, pending or unmeasurable, or the outer mapping is not affine.
A thread whose pin is hidden stays listed and navigable.
A thread with an invalid anchor draws no pin anywhere, and its hint stays inert until the same Widget resolves again.
Pins are drawn only for threads whose Variant scope is empty or includes the current Variant.
Workspace threads have no pin and never appear on a View's canvas or in its Comments list.
Dismissed threads never draw pins, even when the canvas shows resolved threads.
A comment's click point is transient: it only positions the composer, and the server never receives it except as a derived pin hint.

features.title: View Spec Decisions
features.summary: Decisions recorded in a View's Spec: their identity, lifecycle and history, the derived lists of pending Decisions, and explicit promotion of a Review thread into a Decision.

rules.statement: A View's Decisions all live in that View's Spec, in one list whatever their status; pending, deferred and decided lists are derived views, never separate stores.
A Decision keeps its identity through every status change; deferring, deciding or reopening never moves or re-creates it.
A Decision's status changes only through explicit lifecycle actions, never implicitly.
Reopening a decided Decision clears its current outcome, and the earlier outcome survives only in its history.
Every status or outcome change appends a history entry recording its time, its actor or source and the state before and after, so a Decision's lifecycle never depends on Git.
The Workbench derives a cross-View list of pending Decisions from the View files and navigates from each item to its View, and to its Variant or Widget when known.
Review and Decision lifecycles are independent: no reply, resolution or reopen creates, settles or changes a Decision, and promotion never changes the thread's status.
A Review thread becomes a Decision only through an explicit promotion by a human or Agent; comments are never turned into Decisions automatically.
A thread is promoted only into the View it is anchored to.
A Workspace thread cannot be promoted; it must first be re-anchored to a View's RootShell.
A promoted Decision starts pending unless the promotion records an outcome, which makes it decided.
A promoted Decision records its source thread's identity, and the Workbench navigates from the Decision back to that thread.
Promoting a thread that already has a Decision in its View returns that Decision instead of creating a duplicate.
That idempotent return comes before revision checks, so retrying a committed promotion with its original expected revisions succeeds.
Creating another, independent Decision from the same thread requires a distinct explicit action.
Promotion checks the thread's and the View's revisions and adds the Decision to the View in one atomic commit, leaving the thread unchanged.
Promote and resolve stay two actions with their own revision checks: there is no compound promote-and-resolve action and no promoted resolution kind.
When a promotion conflicts, the Workbench names which resource moved, the thread or the View, re-reads and asks the user to confirm again.

features.title: UX Flow graph
features.summary: The UX Flow graph: steps and their View and Variant targets, Widget-Event transitions and their identity, graph validity, invalid references, the external scenario reference, and the Workbench graph editor.

rules.statement: A UX Flow is a design and prototype specification, not a production router: UIUX generates no navigation code from it.
A step that names no Variant targets its View's canonical base state: the View IR and plugin defaults with no Variant preset applied.
A transition is triggered by a semantic Widget Event occurrence, identified by its source Widget and declared Event name; Widget Methods and DOM events are never navigation triggers.
Transitions match only a Widget Event's identity, never its arguments, so branching needs distinct semantic Events.
Within one step a Widget Event trigger leads to at most one transition; a duplicate trigger is a validation error, never resolved by order or priority.
A transition has no identity of its own: its source step and trigger identify it, and the editor's edge keys are temporary.
Every step must be reachable from the entry step; an unreachable step is kept for repair but is a validation error that blocks complete execution and formal Evidence.
Cycles and self-loops are valid, and a step without outgoing transitions is terminal without any flag.
Invalid View, Variant and Widget references are preserved verbatim with structured diagnostics and never rebound by name, type, selector, position or similarity.
A remaining invalid step or transition reference blocks complete execution, formal Flow Evidence and executable Handoff claims, while the Flow stays editable and its valid steps previewable.
Flow validation never checks a trigger's Event name against the Widget's declared Events, so an undeclared Event stays valid.
UIUX never imports, mirrors, authors, synchronizes or validates the scenario a Flow's scenario reference points to, and failing to resolve it never changes the Flow.
The Workbench edits a Flow in a node-and-edge graph editor backed directly by the one canonical Flow, with structured editing of the selected step or transition.
When a trigger Widget's declared Events are known, the Flow editor offers them in a picker, and an existing undeclared Event stays selected and labelled, never cleared or rebound.
Agents can validate a Flow and play it back through MCP Tools, besides creating, reading, listing and updating it.

features.title: Prototype playback
features.summary: The Workbench Prototype player: playing a UX Flow from its entry step with a fresh View Runtime per step entry, following reported Widget Events or Workbench-driven advances, and what playback never observes or keeps.

rules.statement: The Prototype player starts at the Flow's entry step and follows the same canonical Flow the editor edits; UIUX keeps no second prototype model.

Every step entry, including a return to the same step, a self-loop or a restart, creates a fresh View Runtime from the View IR, plugin defaults and the step's Variant, and leaving the step disposes it.
Interactive state may change within a step but never carries across a step boundary.
The Workbench player resolves each reported Widget Event against the Flow; the Preview never receives the Flow and never reports a step.
Only the current step's outgoing triggers are observed, and only while a player has armed the Preview; nothing is observed on the ordinary View canvas.
Each step entry accepts at most one transition from any source; a later occurrence, double click or racing advance for that entry is discarded.
The player learns only which armed Widget Event occurred, never its arguments or the input that caused it.
Playback history stays in the browser: it is never written to the Workspace, sent to the server, or included in Review, Evidence or Handoff.
The player always offers a labelled, keyboard-reachable Next control for each outgoing transition, even when the Preview reports Widget Events.
A Workbench-driven advance is a player action, not a Widget Event: it invokes no Widget Method, synthesizes no input and is never formal Evidence.
Commenting during playback is allowed: in comment mode Widget Events cannot advance the player, and Events from that time are never replayed afterwards.
Nothing observes Widget Events that no transition references, and there is no Event log while authoring a Flow.
When the Preview cannot report Widget Events, the player works through its Next controls alone and says so.

features.title: Formal UX Flow Evidence
features.summary: Formal Evidence for a UX Flow: the replayable traversal trace and its captures, the Evidence-owned replay recipe and its immutability, and how Review and Handoff use Flow Evidence.

rules.statement: Formal UX Flow Evidence is a deterministic, replayable trace with its required Playwright captures, recording the entry context and, per traversed step, its identity, View and Variant, triggering Widget Event, resulting step, validation result and Evidence references.
UIUX executes and verifies the playback with Playwright; a manual screenshot sequence or prose walkthrough is never formal Flow Evidence.
A trace identifies each transition by its source step, trigger and resulting step, never by a transition ID.
The Playwright actions and assertions that drive a replay belong to the Evidence record, never to the Flow or to Adapter Event metadata.
A replay must show that its recorded actions produce the expected Widget Event and transition, so the Evidence proves the semantic transition rather than browser operations.
A replay recipe is immutable with its Evidence: changing it creates new Evidence, and a copied earlier recipe is only an authoring starting point.
A Handoff manifest references Flow traces and captures as derived artifacts, while the canonical Flow is an authored Handoff resource.
A Review submission may name UX Flow as a change domain and reference specific Flows and their traces.

contracts.title: Workspace persisted format
contracts.summary: The persisted format of a UIUX Workspace, versioned as a whole by the manifest `schemaVersion`: the manifest, the path, file unit and identity of every canonical resource kind and of the content-addressed derived-artifact store, the canonical JSON shapes of those resources, and the diagnostics of a Workspace whose schema is older or unsupported.

clauses.statement: The Workspace manifest is `.uiux/workspace.json` under the Workspace root. The `.uiux/` directory is reserved for UIUX system metadata, such as the manifest and the derived-artifact store.

The manifest is a JSON object holding the Workspace-level settings: `schemaVersion`, `i18n`, the ordered `adapters` list and the `viewports` and `themes` registries. All five are required; an empty `adapters` list or registry is valid.

`schemaVersion` is a positive integer and the only schema version in a Workspace: resource files carry none and are all decoded under it. The current version is 3; versions 1 and 2 are recognized older versions.
The migration steps are `uiux.v1-to-v2`, from `schemaVersion` 1 to 2, and `uiux.v2-to-v3`, from 2 to 3.
A field introduced by a later schema version is invalid (`schema.unknown_field`) in a Workspace at an earlier version; no version treats a later version's field as an optional addition.

A Workspace whose schema is `unsupported` is reported with the diagnostic `workspace.schema_unsupported`, which is also the code of every operation refused because of it; an operation refused because the Workspace needs migration reports `workspace.migration_required`. Over HTTP, formal capture, Handoff readiness assessment and Handoff export refused with `workspace.migration_required` answer 422.

`i18n` is an object whose required `defaultLocale` is a canonical BCP 47 tag. Supported Locales are discovered from Locale files and not listed in the manifest, and `i18n` gains further settings only additively, through schema evolution.

`adapters` is an ordered array whose order is the canonical installation order. Each entry holds a portable module reference (a bare package or module specifier, or a `./` specifier relative to the Workspace root; never an absolute or resolved path) and an optional JSON-compatible Adapter `config`.

`viewports` maps viewport IDs to presets. A viewport ID is a non-empty, case-sensitive, opaque Workspace-local string, and each preset records the exact CSS viewport width and height; labels and other metadata are separate from identity.
`themes` maps theme IDs, which are non-empty, case-sensitive, opaque Workspace-local strings, to theme entries; Adapters validate or map those IDs but do not own them.
Each View is one file `views/<uuid>.view.json`, where `<uuid>` is the View's full UUID and equals its `id`.

A View's top level has exactly `id` (its full UUID), `name` (its required display name), an optional single-valued `feature` tag, `ir`, `variants` and `spec`; derived timestamps, file paths or filenames and a generic `metadata` object are not canonical fields.

`ir` is the RootShell Widget, with type `RootShell`, ID `root` and one Slot, `content`: an ordered array of child Widget sources whose own shape the Adapters' Widget plugins define, and which is empty for an empty View.

`variants` is an object keyed by Variant name, a non-empty string. Each entry is `{ state }`, where `state` maps Widget IDs to sparse maps of State member overrides (`variants.<name>.state.<widgetId>.<member>`); entries carry no UUID and do not repeat the name, and the entry object stays open to additive metadata.

`spec` always contains `intent` (a string), `entryConditions`, `interactionRules`, `constraints` and `accessibility` (string lists whose items carry no IDs), `references` (typed references) and `decisions` (Decisions).

Each `references` entry is a typed reference discriminated by `type`: `{ type: "view", viewId, variantName?, relation? }` with a full View UUID as `viewId`, or `{ type: "external", uri, label?, relation? }` with a non-empty absolute URI of any scheme as `uri`. An optional `relation` is a non-empty string, and other `type` values are invalid until a schema version adds them.

A Decision is `{ id, question, status, outcome?, history, provenance? }`: `id` is a full UUID, `question` a string and `status` `pending`, `deferred` or `decided`; `outcome` `{ summary, rationale }`, with a non-empty `summary` and a string `rationale`, is present exactly when `status` is `decided`.

A Decision `history` entry is `{ at, actor?, source?, before, after }` with an `actor` or a `source`; `before` and `after` are `{ status, outcome? }` snapshots, each entry's `before` equals the previous entry's `after`, and the last `after` equals the current status and outcome.
Decision transitions are `pending` ↔ `deferred`, `pending` → `decided`, `deferred` → `decided` and `decided` → `pending`; a reopen's `before` keeps the prior outcome and its `after` has none.
`provenance`, when present, is a JSON object; a Decision promoted from a Review thread records that thread's ID in it as both `reviewId` and `sourceReviewThreadId`.
Each UX Flow is one file `flows/<uuid>.flow.json`, where `<uuid>` equals the Flow's `id`.

A UX Flow is `{ id, name, scenarioRef?, entryStepId, steps }`: `id` is its full UUID, `name` a required non-empty display name, `entryStepId` the full UUID of one of its steps and `steps` an object keyed by full step UUIDs; there is no top-level `transitions` array.

A step entry is `{ target: { viewId, variantName? }, transitions }` and does not repeat its key as `id`; each transition is exactly `{ trigger: { widgetId, event }, targetStepId }`, with no ID or `sourceStepId`, and transition order carries no meaning.

`scenarioRef`, when present, is a JSON object naming an external system or source and an opaque external ID or URI, optionally with a non-authoritative display label; UIUX does not validate its members.
Each Review thread is one file `reviews/<uuid>.review.json`, where `<uuid>` equals the thread's `id`.

A Review thread is a JSON object with exactly `id` (its full UUID), `anchor`, `variantNames` (an array of unique non-empty Variant names), an optional `displayHint`, `status` and the ordered arrays `messages`, `history` and `submissions`.

`anchor` is either the Widget anchor `{ viewId, widgetId }`, with a full View UUID and a non-empty Widget ID, or the Workspace anchor `{ scope: "workspace" }`. Both arms are closed; an object with `scope` is the Workspace arm, and any other `scope` value is `review.invalid_anchor_scope`.

A Workspace-anchored thread has `variantNames: []` (`review.workspace_anchor_variants`) and no `displayHint` (`review.display_hint_without_widget`); the same holds for the Workspace arm inside re-anchor events.
`status` is `open`, `ready-for-review` or `resolved`.
Every message, message edit, submission and history event records an `actor` `{ type, id?, displayName? }` and an authored time `at`, an RFC 3339 UTC timestamp.

A message is `{ id, actor, at, body, edits? }`: `id` is a full UUID and `body` the current text; `edits`, when present, is a non-empty array (`review.message_edits_empty`) of closed `{ id, actor, at, previousBody }` entries, each with a full UUID `id`.

An edited message has an `actor.id`, every edit's `actor` has the message's `actor.id` and `actor.type` (`review.message_edit_not_author`), and edit times strictly follow the message's `at` and never decrease (`review.message_edit_out_of_order`).

No submission and no event entering `resolved` has an `at` between a message's `at` and an edit's `at`, inclusive (`review.message_edit_after_formal_act`); an edited message's `body` is non-empty after trimming (`review.message_body_empty`); and each `previousBody` differs from the text that replaced it (`review.message_edit_noop`).

A submission is `{ id, actor, at, changeDomains, resources, scope, evidenceRefs }`: a full UUID `id`, at least one change domain, at least one resource `{ identity, revision }`, a `scope` object and at least one Evidence reference; its `at` equals the time of the lifecycle event that created it.

Each `evidenceRefs` entry is exactly `{ kind, evidence }`: `kind` is the Evidence taxonomy discriminator and `evidence` the referenced immutable Evidence record's `sha256:<hex>` identity; an entry has no ID, label or other metadata.

A history event has a full UUID `id`, `kind` `lifecycle` or `reanchor`, `actor`, `at` and an optional `reason`. A lifecycle event adds `from`, `to`, an optional `submissionId` and an optional `resolution`; a re-anchor event adds `before` and `after`, each `{ anchor, variantNames }`.

Lifecycle transitions are `open` → `ready-for-review`, `ready-for-review` → `open`, `resolved` → `open`, `ready-for-review` → `resolved` with any resolution and `open` → `resolved` with any resolution but `verified`; any other is `review.invalid_transition`, and the first lifecycle event starts from `open` (`review.invalid_initial_status`).

`resolution` is `verified`, `answered`, `wont-fix`, `duplicate` or `obsolete` (`review.invalid_resolution`), present exactly on lifecycle events entering `resolved` (`review.resolution_required`, `review.resolution_unexpected`); a thread's current resolution is that of its final lifecycle event while it is resolved, never stored separately.

On an event entering `resolved`: `verified` comes from `ready-for-review` and carries the active submission's `submissionId` (`review.resolve_missing_submission`, `review.resolve_stale_submission`); any other resolution has no `submissionId` (`review.direct_resolve_submission_forbidden`); `duplicate` has a non-empty `reason` (`review.resolution_reason_required`); and the actor's `type` is `human` (`review.resolve_requires_human`).

`displayHint` is a closed object with at least one member (`review.display_hint_empty`); its only member, `pin`, is a closed `{ x, y }` of finite numbers from 0 to 1 inclusive (`review.display_hint_out_of_range`), normalized against the anchored Widget's full rendered rectangle with the origin at its top-left, x rightward and y downward.
Writers clamp pin coordinates to [0, 1] and quantize them to 4 fractional digits; validators check only the range and never repair a value.

Each Locale is one file `i18n/<locale>.json`, named by its canonical BCP 47 tag, holding one flat JSON object that maps literal message keys to string values: `.` in a key has no nesting or namespace meaning, and there are no per-View, split or merged Locale files.
Locale files are discovered from `i18n/*.json`; a file whose name is not a canonical BCP 47 tag is diagnosed and excluded from the discovered Locales, never aliased to or merged with another file.
Each authored Asset is one directory `assets/<uuid>/` containing `asset.json` and exactly one source-content file; the directory UUID equals the `id` in `asset.json`.
`asset.json` records at least the Asset `id`, a required display `name`, the source-content filename and the declared `mediaType`; references never depend on display, original or content filenames.
View data binds an Asset only as `{ "$asset": "<assetId>" }`, and only in Adapter Catalog fields declared asset-capable.
Authored Assets under `assets/` are source data; UIUX-generated derived artifacts live separately under `.uiux/artifacts/`.
A derived artifact is identified by `sha256:<hex>` over its bytes and stored immutably under `.uiux/artifacts/sha256/`: identical bytes deduplicate, and an existing blob is never overwritten.

Formal Evidence records are themselves immutable artifacts in that store; there is no mutable `evidence/` resource namespace, and rerunning Evidence creates a new artifact rather than overwriting one.

contracts.title: Mutation and revision semantics
contracts.summary: The semantics every canonical mutation shares on every transport (`/api/*`, `/mcp` and the Workbench): opaque content-derived revisions, the required `expectedRevision`, all-or-nothing conflicts that report the current revision, compact mutation results, the meaning of refusal statuses and the refusal codes of Review actions, how the shared result surfaces over HTTP and MCP, and the change events that commits emit to Workbenches.

clauses.statement: Every mutable canonical resource has an opaque revision derived from its canonical content. Reads and queries return it; it is the same across process restarts and changes whenever that content changes, including through an edit made outside UIUX. Callers must not infer meaning from its representation.
Every mutation of an existing resource carries the `expectedRevision` its caller last read for that resource; a Review action carries its thread's.
A create carries no `expectedRevision`. It names or receives the identity of the new resource, and when a resource with that identity already exists it writes nothing and returns `already_exists`.

When the resource's current revision differs from `expectedRevision`, the whole mutation writes nothing and returns a `conflict` result carrying `currentRevision`; the caller must re-read and decide again.

A successful mutation returns its status, `created`, `updated` or `deleted`, and the affected identity. `created` and `updated` also return the new revision and diagnostics; `deleted`, the result of retracting a Review thread, carries no revision. A result never carries the whole Workspace.
A successful mutation result also carries a summary of what changed.
Competing writes are never merged automatically, by implicit merge, CRDT or OT: the later writer gets a conflict and must re-read, retry or rework explicitly.

Refusals are told apart by status: `conflict` means re-read, `blocked` means a precondition refuses the operation, and `locked` means another member holds an edit lease on the resource, so retry later or ask the holder.
A lease refusal is `{ status: "locked", key, code: "resource.locked", message, lock: { kind, key, holder: { nickname, kind }, expiresAt } }`; it names the holder only by nickname and member kind.
A persistence-busy refusal has the code `persistence.busy`; over HTTP it answers 503 with a `Retry-After` header.
Over HTTP the structured result is the JSON response body; `conflict` and `already_exists` answer 409, and `locked` answers 423.
Over MCP a tool returns the structured result as its structured content (and as JSON text), and any outcome other than success is an error result (`isError`).
HTTP and MCP run an operation through the same application service and return the same result for it; only the transport envelope differs.

The change-event stream is the server-sent events route `GET /api/events`. On connect it sends `hello` with the server instance ID; it sends `resource.changed` (kind, key, revision) or `resource.removed` (kind, key) for a resource, `lock.changed` (kind, key) for a lease and `access.changed` for the roster or the member's role, and a heartbeat comment about every 20 seconds.

Marking a thread ready is refused with `review.target_view_missing` for a target View that does not exist, `review.target_view_revision_missing` when a Widget thread's resources lack its View's current revision, `review.target_workspace_revision_missing` when a Workspace thread's resources lack the current manifest revision, `review.resource_revision_not_current` for a named View not at its current revision, and `review.formal_evidence_not_current` for formal-capture Evidence not complete for its View's current revision.
On a Workspace thread, setting a pin hint is refused with `review.display_hint_without_widget` and promotion with `review.decision_target_unavailable`.

Editing a message is refused with `review.unknown_message` for a message the thread does not have, `review.message_edit_not_author` when the requester is not its author, `review.message_frozen`, naming the submission or resolution that froze it, for a frozen message, `review.message_body_empty` for empty text and `review.message_edit_noop` for unchanged text.

Retraction is refused with `review.retract_not_author` when the requester is not the author of the thread's message, and with `review.retract_engaged` when the thread is engaged, carrying `reason` `status`, `messages`, `history`, `submissions` or `promoted`.
A promotion conflict lists, in `conflicts`, each resource whose revision moved, `review` or `view`, with its key and its expected and current revision.

contracts.title: MCP interface
contracts.summary: The Model Context Protocol surface that Agents use against one selected Workspace: the `/mcp` endpoint and its bearer authentication, the read-only Resources, the discovery, authoring, Review, Evidence, Handoff and lease Tools, and the per-request instructions.

clauses.statement: MCP is served at `/mcp` on the selected Workspace's `uiux dev` server.
A `/mcp` request reaches a Tool or Resource only with a valid member Token.

On `/mcp`, the message of an authentication failure names the fix: create a Token with `uiux token create` and send it as a bearer Token, or, for a Token of another Workspace's roster, create one for this Workspace or run `uiux access copy`.
UIUX advertises no OAuth metadata: every `/.well-known/*` path answers a JSON 404.
On the LAN listener `/mcp` refuses a Token created without the LAN flag with HTTP 403 `auth.lan_not_allowed`.
The per-request server instructions begin with "Authenticated as <nickname> (<kind>, <role>)." for the authenticated member.

MCP Resources are read-only, and no mutation is exposed as a Resource write: the selected Workspace, each View, UX Flow, Locale, Review thread and authored Asset by its canonical key, and each derived artifact by its `sha256:` digest. Reading one that does not exist is a not-found error.

`list_resources` lists, and `search_resources` searches with a non-empty query, the Views, UX Flows, Locales, Review threads and authored Assets, optionally filtered by kind and, for Review threads, by resolution and anchor scope. Both take a required page `limit` and an opaque `cursor`, and each item carries its kind, key, revision, diagnostic count, a kind-specific summary and its Resource URI.

The Review filters of `list_resources` and `search_resources` are `resolution`, a non-empty list of resolution kinds matching only resolved threads whose current resolution is listed, and `anchorScope`, a non-empty list of `workspace` and `view` (any Widget anchor); either filter excludes other resource kinds, and the search term `workspace` matches Workspace threads.

`create_view` creates a View with the canonical empty RootShell IR, no Variants and no Decisions; `update_view_spec` replaces the descriptive Spec fields, keeping Decisions and every non-Spec field; `update_view_structure` replaces the IR and Variants together, keeping the View's identity, name, `feature` tag and Spec.
`update_workspace_settings` updates the manifest-owned Workspace settings (`i18n.defaultLocale`, `adapters`, `viewports` and `themes`) and keeps `schemaVersion`.
`create_locale` creates a Locale file named by a canonical BCP 47 tag and fails if it exists; `update_locale` updates an existing Locale's messages.
`create_flow` creates a UX Flow (identity, entry step and step transition graph) and fails if it exists; `update_flow` updates one, keeping its identity.
`create_asset` creates an authored Asset from its metadata and source content; `replace_asset` replaces an authored Asset, keeping its identity.

The Review tools are `create_review_thread`, `append_review_message`, `reanchor_review_thread`, `set_review_display_hint`, `submit_ready_for_review`, `reopen_review_thread`, `promote_review_to_decision`, `edit_review_message` and `retract_review_thread`; each atomically changes one Review thread (promotion also writes the target View's Decisions).

`resolve_review_thread` stays registered but always refuses: a human member gets `review.resolve_requires_workbench`, an Agent asking for a resolution other than `verified` gets `review.direct_resolve_requires_workbench`, and any other Agent gets `review.resolve_requires_human`.

`capture_formal_evidence` captures formal Evidence for an explicit list of resolved render contexts; `assess_handoff_readiness` assesses explicit Handoff roots without exporting; `export_handoff` exports an immutable Handoff bundle from explicit roots.

`acquire_lock` takes `{ resources: [{ kind, key }] }` with 1 to 16 entries and is all-or-nothing: it returns `{ status: "acquired", leases: [{ kind, key, expiresAt }] }`, or `locked` naming every conflicting lease. `release_lock` takes optional `resources` (omitted means all of the caller's leases), is idempotent and returns the released list.

## Notes

- Why a Contract: MCP is the external agent interface; agents and their configurations depend on it independently of any one Feature.
- Owner ruling 2026-10-07 (checkpoint C): tool input and output field shapes are authoritative in code at 20c427c (`src/mcp/server.ts` zod schemas); the Clauses fix which tools and Resources exist and what they do. The Review-specific semantics of the Review tools belong to the Review Features (import batch 4); the Review discovery filters are {{C.mcp.review-filters}}.
- The MCP transport is the SDK's stateless per-request HTTP handler; that choice is implementation detail.
